rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: The youths, the Companions of the Cave, fled to God for the sake of their religion.
rows.anchor: fleeing to God for the sake of their religion (IK, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Th, Ṭs
rows.claim: They sought refuge from King Daqyānūs, also called Daqyūs in another report.
rows.anchor: seeking refuge from a king named Daqyānūs (Th, Ṭs) or Daqyūs (Q)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Daqyānūs may Arabize Decius, the king in the Christian account who tried to force idol worship.
rows.anchor: which may be an Arabization of Decius, the name of the king in the Christian account, who was attempting to force his subjects to worship idols (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī also reports a possibility from some Christian sources that the persecuting king was Zoroastrian.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabrisī also mentions the possibility, as suggested in some Christian sources, that it was a Zoroastrian king trying to force his Christian subjects to follow his religion (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs, Q
rows.claim: Some accounts place the youths among the king’s courtiers; another says they were sons of local noble families.
rows.anchor: the youths, who may have been among the king’s courtiers (Ṭs) or the sons of local noble families (Q)

rows.speaker: Th, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some reports say the youths lived in Ephesus and hid their belief from fear of persecution.
rows.anchor: Some report that the youths, who may have been among the king’s courtiers (Ṭs) or the sons of local noble families (Q), lived in Ephesus and were believers hiding their faith out of fear of persecution (Th, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Others identify them as Christians preserving their faith and practices amid corruption, oppressive rule, and idolatry.
rows.anchor: Others indicate that they were Christians attempting to maintain the beliefs and practices of Christianity at a time of great religious corruption, oppressive kings, and a turn toward idolatry (Th)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: After learning they were in a cave, the king sealed its entrance, expecting hunger and thirst to kill them.
rows.anchor: the king eventually learned that the youths had sought refuge in a cave. He thus had the entrance to the cave sealed, thinking that they would die of hunger and thirst (Th)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The mercy they requested from God’s Presence is explained as coming from His storehouse of Mercy.
rows.anchor: from God’s storehouse of Mercy (R, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Their prayer sought guidance, knowledge, provision, patience, safety from enemies, and eventual deliverance.
rows.anchor: God would grant them guidance and knowledge, provision, patience in their trial, security from their enemies, and eventual deliverance (R, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Their prayer is compared with a hadith prayer asking God to make the ends of all affairs virtuous.
rows.anchor: as in the prayer of the Prophet reported in a ḥadīth, “O God, make virtuous the ends of all our affairs” (IK)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some say they asked God eventually to grant them a safe way out of the cave.
rows.anchor: praying that God would eventually grant them a safe exit from the cave (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The cave is where they withdrew after despairing of the world’s kindness and sought God’s protection alone.
rows.anchor: having despaired of its kindness, and sought the protection of God alone (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mystical interpretation makes the cave a symbol of the heart.
rows.anchor: From a mystical perspective, the cave represents the heart.

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Some reports say the youths spent their cave years praying, praising God, and devoting themselves to Him.
rows.anchor: the youths spent their time in the cave praying and praising God and devoting themselves fully to Him (Th)

rows.speaker: ST
rows.claim: For some, asking for mercy meant asking God to preserve them through His remembrance.
rows.anchor: their plea for mercy was a plea for God to preserve them in or through the remembrance of Him (ST)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prolonged life can symbolize remembrance that takes a person beyond ordinary time.
rows.anchor: the extended life of the youths of the cave can be seen as symbolic of this experience.

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The phrase literally says God struck them upon the ears, preventing sounds from waking them.
rows.anchor: literally, “struck them upon the ears,” meaning that He made them incapable of hearing sounds that could awaken them (R, Z)

rows.speaker: IK, Th, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God put them into a very deep slumber.
rows.anchor: that He put them into a very deep slumber (IK, Th, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: A number of years can designate either a long or a short period.
rows.anchor: A number of years may refer to a long or short period of time (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 25 gives their sleep as 309 years, yet they experienced it as a day or part of one in verse 19.
rows.anchor: v. 25 gives the number of years as 309, but the Companions of the Cave experienced this long amount of time as but a day or part of a day (v. 19)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The description indicates they remained asleep and did not die.
rows.anchor: the companions did not die, but remained in a deep sleep (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Raising the youths means awakening them from sleep.
rows.anchor: Raised them means awakened them from their sleep (R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that God raised them to know appears to challenge divine foreknowledge; Quranic test language can mean God tests people while already knowing the answer.
rows.anchor: although God might test people in order to know something, He already has the answer prior to the accomplishment of the test

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: The two parties may be two groups among the Companions themselves.
rows.anchor: two groups among the companions themselves (see v. 19; R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another view identifies the parties as the Companions and the kings who ruled the city.
rows.anchor: the companions and the kings who reigned over the city (R)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: A further view takes the parties to be everyone who differed over how long the youths stayed.
rows.anchor: all those who differed regarding this matter (IK)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Sufis take the verse as evidence that saints may receive karāmāt, miracles distinct from prophetic muʿjizāt.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that the Sufis understand this verse to be proof that, besides the evidentiary miracles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic texts clearly distinguish prophetic evidentiary miracles from miracles granted to saints or friends of God.
rows.anchor: These two kinds of miracles are clearly distinguished in Islamic texts.

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The Quran stresses the Companions’ youth; some commentators say the young are more likely to follow prophets while elders cling to false religion.
rows.anchor: it is often the youth of a community who are most likely to respond to the messages of the prophets, while the elders of the community are more entrenched in their false religious practices (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Younger Quraysh members were more likely than their elders to follow the Prophet.
rows.anchor: it was the younger members of the Quraysh who were more likely to follow the Prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s youthful faith contrasts with his father’s idolatry; elsewhere community notables reject prophets.
rows.anchor: juxtaposes the faith of the youthful Abraham against the idolatry of his father and the leaders of his people

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: The word fatiyyah for youths is related to futuwwah, spiritual chivalry grounded in faith.
rows.anchor: which is based upon faith (Q, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Q, Su
rows.claim: Futuwwah includes virtue, generosity, avoiding forbidden acts and harm, patience, truthfulness, freedom from hypocrisy, and detachment from worldly ties.
rows.anchor: being virtuous and generous, refraining from what is forbidden and from harming others, never complaining about one’s situation (Q), being true to one’s word, avoiding all hypocrisy, and cutting oneself off from all (worldly) attachments (Su)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term futuwwah later became associated with guilds that cultivated these virtues.
rows.anchor: Later this term became associated with guilds in which these virtues were cultivated.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One interpretation of increased guidance is an increase in the youths’ faith.
rows.anchor: meaning their faith was increased (Q)

rows.speaker: ST, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation is greater understanding and discernment through faith, along with patience to endure separation from their people.
rows.anchor: greater understanding and discernment of the truth through faith (ST) as well as the patience to endure separation from their people (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran says God increases tendencies already shown: disease for the unrepentant and faith for believers, including increased guidance.
rows.anchor: God increases the tendencies already manifested by human beings: if the diseased of heart do not turn to God, their disease is increased

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: God fortified their hearts by strengthening their patience and faith.
rows.anchor: strengthening them in patience and faith (R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Another account adds that God strengthened their certitude.
rows.anchor: and also certitude (Qu)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Their rising refers to openly defying Daqyānūs and refusing his demand that they worship false deities.
rows.anchor: the youths’ open defiance of the tyrant king Daqyānūs and his demand that they worship his false deities (R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: They declared their Lord rules heaven and earth, while the tyrant’s false deities are merely subjects of the one Lord.
rows.anchor: more than the subjects of the one Lord(Ṭ).

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: In another account, the youths privately held belief in one God; their eldest confessed it when they met by chance outside the city.
rows.anchor: the youths secretly harbored their belief in one God independently of one other. When the group happened to meet by chance outside the city on one occasion, the eldest of them confessed to his belief in one God (IK, R)

rows.speaker: R, IK
rows.claim: Finding the others agreed, they proclaimed their faith either immediately or after returning to the king’s court.
rows.anchor: finding the others in agreement, they collectively uttered the proclamation about their Lord in v. 14, either there and then (R) or after they had returned to the court of the king (IK)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The words are attributed to Tamlīkhā, also called Yamlīkhā or Iamblichus, the reported leader of the youths.
rows.anchor: These are the words of Tamlīkhā (or Yamlīkhā, Iamblichus) the reported chief of the youths (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamlīkhā tells the youths to hide from disbelievers by taking refuge in the cave.
rows.anchor: He instructs them to take refuge in the cave, to hide themselves from the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The youths’ retreat parallels the Prophet and Abū Bakr hiding in a cave during the Hijrah while fleeing the pursuing Makkans.
rows.anchor: as they sought to elude the pursuing Makkans (see 9:40 and commentary; IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In both episodes the cave symbolizes the heart’s interior, providing miraculous sanctuary and refuge from worldly evils.
rows.anchor: the cave, which is a symbol of the interior“space” of the heart, offers miraculous sanctuary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of ease answers the youths’ prayer for sound judgment in their affair in verse 10.
rows.anchor: suggests a response to the youths’ supplication to God in v. 10 that He make them incline to sound judgment in their affair.

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī takes the address as directed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: according to al-Ṭabarī, although others consider it to be addressed to an unspecified interlocutor (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Others understand the verse as addressed to an unspecified interlocutor rather than the Prophet.
rows.anchor: others consider it to be addressed to an unspecified interlocutor (Q, R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The sun’s movement away at sunrise and sunset can be read as parallel despite the different wording.
rows.anchor: despite the different phrases, these movements can be understood as parallel to one another (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, Z
rows.claim: The cave’s open space means it was spacious, with a broad opening that let fresh air and cool breezes reach the youths.
rows.anchor: the cave was spacious with a broad opening that allowed fresh air and cool breezes to reach the youths as they slept within it (IK, JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th, Z
rows.claim: Because the sun slanted away, the youths avoided direct heat and stayed comfortably in shade.
rows.anchor: the slanting of the sun away from the cave meant that they did not suffer from the heat of direct sunlight, but remained comfortably in the shade (Ṭ, Th, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shade is a divine blessing in this life and especially the Hereafter; the Quran also names shade and mountain refuges among God’s blessings.
rows.anchor: In the Quran, shade is one of God’s blessings in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s pairing of divine guidance and misguidance is discussed through cross-referenced commentary.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of this idea and the respective fates of those involved, see 7:178c; 17:97c.

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Their seeming awake despite sleeping may reflect open eyes or turning once or twice yearly.
rows.anchor: perhaps because they slept with their eyes open or because of their turning, which some suggested occurred once or twice a year (R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their appearance may indicate a state between ordinary waking and sleep.
rows.anchor: This may indicate that they were in an intermediate state between ordinary waking and sleeping.

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A well-known hadith says that people are asleep and awaken when they die, associating worldly wakefulness with sleep and death with full awakening.
rows.anchor: the well-known ḥadīth, “Man is asleep, and when he dies he awakens,” where ordinary awakeness is associated with sleep and death with full awakening

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep and waking can symbolize death and resurrection, as in the verse describing God taking souls at night and resurrecting them by day.
rows.anchor: Sleeping and waking can also serve as metaphors for life and death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep is an intermediate barzakh: the soul is taken while one remains alive, making sleep a minor death and waking a resurrection.
rows.anchor: been“taken” by God (6:60), so that it is a kind of “minor death,” after which waking is like a resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Cave story can allegorize barzakh, the interval between individual death and universal resurrection, as well as prove resurrection.
rows.anchor: the story of the Companions of the Cave can be read not only as a proof of God’s power of resurrection, but also as an allegory for the barzakh

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: From a Sufi perspective, the youths’ turning represents alternation between annihilation and subsistence in God.
rows.anchor: From a Sufi perspective, the turning of the youths in their sleep can also represent their alternation

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: God turned them to prevent the earth from covering and eventually consuming their bodies.
rows.anchor: in order to prevent them from being covered and eventually consumed by the earth (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: Some commentators say the dog served as their hunting animal.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators the dog served as their hunting animal (Th)

rows.speaker: Q, Th
rows.claim: Some say the youths encountered the dog while fleeing, tried to chase it away, and it was miraculously enabled to speak.
rows.anchor: the youths happened to come upon the dog as they were fleeing from the king (Q, Th). They initially tried to chase him off

rows.speaker: Q, R, Th
rows.claim: The speaking dog reportedly said it loved God’s lovers and would keep watch while they slept.
rows.anchor: said to the youths, “I love the lovers of God; so sleep while I keep watch”(Q, R, Th)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another account says a sheepdog and its shepherd followed the youths.
rows.anchor: a sheepdog belonging to a shepherd whom they had met on the way, both of whom followed the youths (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Some identify kalb as a companion’s name, perhaps their cook or dog keeper; another reading kālib yields dog keeper, and “paws” becomes “arms.”
rows.anchor: the word for “dog,” kalb, was actually the name of another individual who accompanied the youths

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Waṣīd translated as threshold can also mean the cave’s door or entrance, or the earth or dust in front of it.
rows.anchor: Threshold translates waṣīd, which can also refer to the door or entrance to the cave or to the earth or dust in front of it (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse addresses the Prophet; God’s fearsome appearance for the youths kept anyone from touching or disturbing them as they slept.
rows.anchor: prevent anyone from touching or disturbing them while they slept(Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The youths awoke after a shepherd opened the cave while seeking shelter for his flock from rain.
rows.anchor: the youths awoke after their cave was discovered by a shepherd looking for a place to shelter his flock from the rain. When he cleared the entrance of the cave, the youths awoke (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Some say they estimated a day because they entered the cave in the morning and awoke at sunset.
rows.anchor: they estimated they had passed a day, since they entered the cave in the morning and awoke at sunset (IK, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Others say they noticed their long hair and nails before concluding that God knew best how long they had slept.
rows.anchor: only upon seeing the length of their hair and nails did they say, Your Lord knows best how long you have tarried (R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their one-day estimate resembles the man awakened after a hundred years and Quranic accounts of people thinking their wait before resurrection was short.
rows.anchor: their estimation of having tarried a day is identical to that made by a man who had doubted the resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel reactions connect the Cave story symbolically with death, resurrection, and the intervening barzakh.
rows.anchor: the close symbolic connection of this story to death, resurrection, and the intermediate state, or barzakh, between them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chosen youth carried a silver dirham stamped with the oppressive king’s image and was told to buy food discreetly to avoid persecution.
rows.anchor: a silver dirham bearing the imprint of the oppressive king of their own time, and to enter the city in order to purchase food; but he was to do this discreetly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The old coin exposed the youth; centuries had passed and the city was ruled by the righteous king Tīdhusīs, or Theodocius.
rows.anchor: the people were amazed to see the old coin. They informed the youth that centuries had passed. They were now ruled by a righteous king, Tīdhusīs (Theodocius; Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The townspeople’s dispute concerned whether resurrection restores the body as well as the spirit or raises only the spirit.
rows.anchor: about whether the body was resurrected along with the spirit or the spirit alone was raised.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous king believed in bodily resurrection and prayed for a sign to persuade his people.
rows.anchor: The king believed in bodily resurrection and prayed to God for a sign to convince his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He presented the youths as proof of bodily and spiritual resurrection, then led people to the cave with the youth.
rows.anchor: he announced it as a sign that resurrection is both a bodily and spiritual reality and, guided by the youth, led a delegation of the people to the cave.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: When the youth rejoined the others, they returned to deep sleep; the king and townspeople later found their bodies perfectly preserved.
rows.anchor: he was instantly returned to his deep sleep, as were his companions. The king and the townsfolk later entered and found them in a state of bodily perfection, without any sign of decomposition (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some versions say the youth spoke briefly with the king and townspeople, bade them well, returned to sleep, and eventually died.
rows.anchor: some indicate that the youth talked briefly with the king and the townspeople, bidding them well, then returned to their state of sleep, and finally died.

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: Some reports say the townsfolk later found tablets listing the youths’ names and story.
rows.anchor: Some report that the townsfolk later found in the cave the tablets bearing the inscription (v. 9) that told the names of the youth and their story (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Their discovery was a sign that God’s promise and the Resurrection are true: raising sleepers unchanged after centuries shows He can raise the dead.
rows.anchor: for one who can raise sleepers unaltered after many centuries can certainly raise the dead (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says they built a structure that later became a place for prayer.
rows.anchor: According to al-Ṭabarī, they erected a building that later become a place of prayer.

rows.speaker: JJ, R
rows.claim: Some say believers favored a place of prayer while disbelievers argued for a building as a memorial.
rows.anchor: in which the disbelievers argued for a building and the believers for a place of prayer (JJ, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other disputes concerned whether the youths were dead or asleep, their time in the cave, or their number; the people deferred to God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: their disagreement regarding the state of the youth, whether they were dead or sleeping, the time they spent in the cave, or their number (see v. 22)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses address the Prophet: do not promise future action, using tomorrow for the future generally, without making fulfillment conditional on God’s will.
rows.anchor: he should never make a promise regarding what he might do tomorrow, meaning the future in general (Z), without acknowledging that its fulfillment depends upon the Will of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context is Muhammad’s promise to answer Meccan questions about the youths the next day; revelation was delayed fifteen days, prompting doubts about his answer and prophethood.
rows.anchor: he did not receive revelation for fifteen days according to some, leading the Makkans to doubt his ability to answer their questions and ultimately to doubt his prophethood (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators read this as an instruction to say “if God wills” with any promise about future action.
rows.anchor: Some commentators suggest that the verse can be read as an instruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims commonly say in shāʾ Allāh about future aims, recalling that nothing lies outside God’s will and the future is in His hands.
rows.anchor: This practice serves as a constant reminder that nothing happens outside the Will of God and acknowledges that the future is firmly in His Hands.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet forgets to acknowledge God’s will, he and all people should remember God again; this calls for recollection rather than regret and resembles 6:68.
rows.anchor: The Quranic injunction here, to respond to forgetfulness of God not with bitter regret, but simply with renewed recollection and correction

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Some say one should correct the omission while still in the place and situation where the original statement was made.
rows.anchor: one realizes one’s error in forgetting to acknowledge the role of God’s Will and corrects oneself while still in the same place and situation in which one made the original statement (JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Others allow saying the formula much later, though one may then owe expiation for an unfulfilled oath.
rows.anchor: one can utter the formula even much later (Ṭ, Z), although one may still be liable for offering expiation for an unfulfilled oath (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expiation discussion points to Quranic instructions on keeping and breaking oaths.
rows.anchor: regarding the importance of keeping oaths, see commentary on 16:91–92; regarding expiation for broken oaths, see 5:89c.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: One reading takes the request for nearer rectitude as the words to say when remembering the forgotten acknowledgment of God’s will.
rows.anchor: may be understood to be the content of the remembrance one makes upon realizing one has forgotten to acknowledge God’s Will in a matter (Z)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, JJ, Z
rows.claim: Another reading makes it the Prophet’s prayer for signs and proofs of prophethood even greater than the information about the Cave youths.
rows.anchor: the Prophet’s prayer that he would be given even greater signs and proofs of his prophethood than that of his having been informed by God about the youths of the cave (Bḍ, JJ, Z)
